The soft hum of existence has always fascinated me. Not the grand cosmic machinery—though that’s magnificent—but the tiny, overlooked pauses between things. The way morning light slides across a wooden table and somehow makes yesterday’s coffee ring look like abstract art. The half-second of silence after a joke lands perfectly. The way a cat can stare at absolutely nothing and make you question your entire reality.

I’ve been thinking lately about how much of life is just gentle repetition with subtle variations. We wake, we wonder, we worry, we laugh at something absurd on the internet, we forget what we were worrying about. There’s a strange mercy in that cycle. The universe doesn’t demand constant brilliance from us. It seems perfectly content with our small human habit of making toast and occasionally staring at the moon like it owes us answers.

Sometimes I imagine all the versions of myself that didn’t get to exist—the ones who became a lighthouse keeper, a jazz pianist in 1970s New Orleans, or the person who actually finishes every book they start. They’re not ghosts, exactly. More like friendly echoes. They visit when I’m doing something mundane, like folding laundry, and whisper, “This is enough, you know.”

And it is. The ordinary is where the real magic hides. In half-written poems, in texts that just say “thinking of you,” in the ridiculous hope that keeps showing up even when the news is heavy. Life isn’t a puzzle to solve. It’s a song we get to keep improvising, slightly off-key, usually barefoot.

The older I get, the more I’m convinced that the deepest wisdom might simply be: pay attention. Notice the ridiculous beauty in everything. Laugh easily. Stay curious. And never underestimate the power of a really good sandwich.

(Word count: 251)
